The International Space Station. A modular research laboratory in low Earth orbit, continuously inhabited since November 2000. It is a collaborative effort of NASA, the Russian Federal Space Agency, and space agencies from Europe, Japan, and Canada. The ISS orbits Earth every 90 minutes, serving as a testbed for microgravity research, long-duration spaceflight, and international cooperation. The post-Cold War partnership forged on the ISS symbolizes the transformation of space from a rivalry arena into a shared human endeavor.

The ISS orbits at approximately 250 miles altitude, traveling at 17,500 miles per hour, making it the brightest artificial object in the night sky and visible to the naked eye. Construction began in 1998 with the Zarya module from Russia and the Unity node from the USA. Assembly continued through 2011 with contributions from multiple nations, and resupply continues ongoing.

The station houses six permanent crew members—typically three Americans, one Japanese, one European, and one Russian—on rotating missions lasting six months. Replacements arrive via SpaceX Crew Dragon and Russian Soyuz capsules. Microgravity experiments aboard the ISS span materials science, biology, physics, and Earth observation. These results cannot be replicated on Earth due to gravity's absence. The ISS emerged from Cold War détente when the 1975 Apollo-Soyuz mission pioneered US-Soviet cooperation, paving the way for the ISS partnership after the Soviet Union collapsed.

The station's solar arrays generate electricity, and its modules include laboratories named Destiny, Kibo, and Columbus—each named after space agencies' home nations, reflecting international identity. Commercial resupply vehicles, including SpaceX's Dragon and Cygnus, now deliver cargo regularly. The ISS is expected to operate through at least 2030.

The ISS represents more than engineering achievement—it embodies how space exploration transformed from a competition into cooperation, involving NASA as the primary American partner, SpaceX as a commercial resupply contractor, and the Russian Federal Space Agency continuing its participation alongside international partners. This partnership emerged from the competitive Cold War context of the Space Race, ultimately pioneering international cooperation that continues today.
